title: Serenus asks for help
hookLine: On Tranquility opens with a friend confessing he is neither sick nor well (On Tranquility 1)

cards: Nothing's wrong, exactly. No crisis. Nobody would call a helpline.
But not okay either. Some days a simple life looks right; other days a scroll through other people's kitchens leaves a person feeling a little poorer. Things get started and dropped.
A restlessness with no name. A friend of Seneca's named Serenus wrote him a letter describing exactly that, and Seneca made it the opening of a whole book, On Tranquility of Mind.
Our first essay starts with somebody else's honesty.

teach.h: NOT FREE, NOT FULLY A SLAVE.
teach.b: First, the confession. When Serenus looks at himself honestly, he says, some faults are out in the open, some are hidden, and some come and go.
He isn't free of the things he dislikes in himself, and he isn't fully their slave either. He's neither sick nor well. Second, the details.

teach.h: PLAIN LIVING, THEN A RICH HOUSE.
teach.b: He loves plain living: a simple servant, plain dishes, nothing for show. Then he visits a rich house, all polished floors and crowds of servants, and comes home not worse, he says, but sadder.
He resolves to go into public life; one setback and he wants to retreat. He decides to write plainly; then grand phrases carry him off. Third, his image.

It isn't a storm that troubles me, Serenus says, it's seasickness: the sea is calm, and still the stomach turns. And then the plainest line of all: if you have any remedy, please. Fourth, Seneca's name for the cure.
What Serenus wants, he answers, is something the Greek thinker Democritus called euthymia, good spirits, a steady mind.
Seneca gives it a Latin name: tranquillitas, calm. Not excitement, not numbness.
A mind on level ground, at peace with itself. Notice how the book begins. Not with a lecture.
With a friend willing to describe, plainly, a trouble he couldn't name.

how: Readers of On Tranquility of Mind sometimes begin, as Serenus did, by describing their own restlessness honestly before looking for any remedy.

o: the friend whose honest letter opens the essay
the Greek thinker who named good spirits euthymia
a Roman general who conquered Sicily

games.q: Serenus asks for help — tap the pairs.
p: not a storm, a calm sea

s: On Tranquility opens with Seneca lecturing his friend
it opens with Serenus' own long confession.
Serenus compares his state to seasickness on a calm sea
not a storm, he says: the stomach turns anyway.
it means a mind on level ground, at peace with itself.

games.q: you're Serenus. nothing is wrong, but you're restless and drifting. what do you do?
o: write to a wise friend and describe it honestly.
make a big change: move, quit, start over.
games.why: he wrote to Seneca, and Seneca answered with a whole book.

practice: Describe your own unsettledness to yourself as precisely as Serenus did, not why, just what it's like: where it shows up, what you want one day and drop the next, whether it's a storm or calm-sea seasickness.
Find one honest sentence, the kind you'd only write to a good friend; naming it is the first page.

wordCard.voice: Serenus. The friend whose honest letter, confessing he's neither sick nor well, opens Seneca's book On Tranquility of Mind. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, 'good spirits': Democritus' word, which Seneca renders in Latin as tranquillitas.

carryVoice: Your line: neither sick nor well. The whole book began with someone asking. That's day four hundred ninety-five.
